---
title: "Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent"
---

> **Scope.** Codex CLI has been open-source since April 2025. This note studies
> the current agent runtime at OpenAI's
> [`openai/codex`](https://github.com/openai/codex) repository, pinned for this
> analysis at commit
> [`aec653d`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8).
> The repository exposes the local harness, protocol, sandboxing, SDKs, and
> supporting services. It does **not** open-source the Codex model weights or
> imply that every hosted service and product interface is present.

Codex is valuable to study because it turns the abstract components in
[Agent Harness](harness.qmd) into a production system. The main lesson is not a
particular prompt. It is how probabilistic model decisions are embedded inside
deterministic state, execution, security, and protocol boundaries.

## 1. Start from the Actual System Boundary

A coding model proposes tokens and structured actions. A coding agent must also
own a workspace, execute processes, preserve history, constrain side effects,
stream progress, accept interruptions, and recover across sessions.

Write the end-to-end system as

$$
\boxed{
\text{Codex system}
=
\text{coding model}
+
\text{Codex harness}
+
\text{execution environment}
+
\text{client or orchestrator}
}.
$$

These parts have different jobs:

| Layer | Responsibility | Learned? |
|---|---|---|
| Model | interpret intent, reason about code, choose actions, synthesize results | mostly |
| Harness | compile context, run the loop, route tools, persist state, enforce policy | mostly not |
| Environment | files, Git state, processes, network, APIs, tests, external consequences | no |
| Client | interaction, review, steering, approval, and presentation | no |
| Orchestrator | assign tasks, isolate workspaces, supervise many agent sessions | possibly hybrid |

The open-source repository is primarily the second layer plus interfaces into
the third and fourth. A model can be replaced behind a compatible Responses API
endpoint, while a client can communicate with the harness through the app-server
protocol. This is an intentional separation of **intelligence**, **mechanism**,
and **product surface**.

## 2. Architecture: One Core, Several Surfaces

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    U[User or orchestrator]
    C[CLI / TUI / IDE / client]
    A[App-server protocol]
    H[Codex core harness]
    M[Responses-compatible model]
    X[Tool router]
    P[Policy and approvals]
    E[Execution environment]
    R[Rollout and state stores]

    U <--> C
    C <--> A
    A <--> H
    H <--> M
    H <--> X
    X --> P
    P --> E
    E --> X
    H <--> R
    H -. events .-> A
```

The diagram is conceptual, not a complete crate dependency graph. The source is
large, but a few regions reveal the design:

| Source area | Architectural role |
|---|---|
| [`codex-rs/core`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/core) | session, turn, context, model, tool, permission, and agent logic |
| [`core/src/session/turn.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/core/src/session/turn.rs) | the model--tool feedback loop |
| [`core/src/tools`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/core/src/tools) | tool specifications, routing, handlers, hooks, and concurrency |
| [`app-server`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/app-server) and [`app-server-protocol`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/app-server-protocol) | UI-independent thread, turn, item, approval, and event API |
| [`rollout`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/rollout) and [`state`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/state) | durable histories, reconstruction, indexing, and metadata |
| [`sandboxing`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/sandboxing) and [`execpolicy`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/execpolicy) | OS isolation and command policy |
| [`skills`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/skills), [`plugins`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/core/src/plugins), and [`rmcp-client`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/rmcp-client) | reusable instructions and external capabilities |

The important design choice is that the harness core is not fused to one UI.
The app-server exposes a typed lifecycle that multiple clients can project into
different experiences.

## 3. Three Nested Timescales

“Agent step” is too ambiguous. Codex distinguishes at least three timescales:

| Unit | Begins with | May contain | Ends with |
|---|---|---|---|
| Thread | starting or resuming a conversation | many turns | archive, delete, or abandonment |
| Turn | new user input | many model samples and tool calls | final assistant message, error, or interruption |
| Sampling step | one model request | streamed items and possibly several tool calls | response completion or retryable failure |

This distinction matters for state ownership:

- model-client routing and some caches can be turn-scoped
- conversation history is thread-scoped
- a tool call belongs to the exact step context that advertised it
- cancellation can stop an in-flight turn without destroying the thread
- steering can append user input while a regular turn is running

The [app-server API](https://developers.openai.com/codex/app-server) makes these
boundaries explicit through operations such as `thread/start`, `thread/resume`,
`turn/start`, `turn/steer`, and `turn/interrupt`.

## 4. The Core Loop

At a high level, Codex runs

```text
record user input and context changes
repeat:
    construct the current model-visible history and tool list
    stream a response from a Responses-compatible endpoint
    record response items and emit client events
    if the response contains tool calls:
        validate, authorize, dispatch, and observe them
        append bounded tool outputs to history
    otherwise:
        finish the turn with the assistant message
until interrupted, failed, or complete
```

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    I[User input] --> W[Capture a consistent step context]
    W --> B[Build prompt: history + instructions + tools]
    B --> S[Stream model response]
    S --> T{Tool call?}
    T -- no --> F[Record final assistant message]
    T -- yes --> V[Parse and route typed call]
    V --> G[Hooks, policy, sandbox, approval]
    G --> E[Execute tool]
    E --> O[Record result and emit events]
    O --> K{Context limit or new input?}
    K -- compact / merge --> B
    K -- continue --> B
```

The real [`run_turn`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/core/src/session/turn.rs)
is more complex because production loops must handle streaming, retries,
compaction, hooks, dynamic tools, pending user input, cancellation, telemetry,
and partial failures. But its invariant remains simple:

$$
\text{model proposal}
\ne
\text{environmental side effect}.
$$

The proposal becomes a side effect only after harness-controlled parsing,
routing, authorization, and execution.

## 5. Context Is Compiled State, Not Just Chat History

Codex's initial model input combines several sources with distinct authority:

1. model-specific base instructions
2. sandbox and approval instructions
3. managed or user developer instructions
4. hierarchical repository instructions such as `AGENTS.md`
5. skill and plugin metadata
6. environment state such as working directory and shell
7. conversation items and the current user request

Repository instructions are discovered from the project root toward the working
directory, so broad rules can be refined by more local ones. This makes context
composition resemble lexical scoping: the effective behavior at a file depends
on the instructions along its path. See OpenAI's
[`AGENTS.md` guide](https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md) and the
source implementation in
[`agents_md.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/core/src/agents_md.rs).

### Context also has a systems cost

For transformer inference, a stable prompt prefix can reuse cached computation.
Consequently, semantically equivalent context layouts need not have equivalent
cost. Codex tries to avoid rewriting earlier history, maintains deterministic
tool ordering, and appends changes to permissions or environment as new items.

A better context objective therefore includes both relevance and prefix
stability:

$$
c_t^*
=
\arg\max_{c_t}
\left[
U(c_t)
-\lambda |c_t|
+\gamma\,\operatorname{ReusablePrefix}(c_{t-1},c_t)
\right].
$$

This produces a general harness principle:

> Treat the prompt prefix like a cache-sensitive interface. Keep stable facts
> stable, order dynamic collections deterministically, and append state changes
> when possible.

### Compaction is state estimation

Conversation history grows until it competes with future reasoning and output
tokens. Codex can replace a long history with a compact representation and then
continue the same thread. Compaction is not mere compression; it estimates the
smallest state sufficient for future decisions:

$$
p(o_{t+1}\mid h_t,a_t)
\approx
p(o_{t+1}\mid \phi(h_t),a_t).
$$

The failure mode is not only losing prose. A bad summary can discard an
unresolved error, user constraint, permission boundary, or the reason an earlier
approach failed. Durable rollouts and external artifacts keep raw evidence
available even when model-visible history is compacted.

## 6. Tools Are Typed Capabilities

The model receives schemas, but the harness owns implementations. Codex's tool
path separates:

1. **specification:** what the model is allowed to request
2. **routing:** which implementation owns the call
3. **lifecycle:** start, stream, finish, abort, and telemetry events
4. **policy:** whether the action may execute
5. **execution:** how it runs and how output is bounded
6. **observation:** the normalized result returned to the model

The [`ToolRouter`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/core/src/tools/router.rs)
maps response items into namespaced typed calls. The registry can combine
built-ins, hosted tools, MCP tools, plugins, and dynamically exposed tools.

### Concurrency is a tool property

Codex does not assume that all tool calls are safe to parallelize. In
[`parallel.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/aec653daa9873bf44517a623fd033722737817a8/codex-rs/core/src/tools/parallel.rs),
parallel-safe calls share a read lock, while a non-parallel call takes the write
lock and excludes the others.

This is a compact concurrency contract:

$$
\text{parallelize}(a_i,a_j)
\iff
\text{their declared effects commute safely}.
$$

The model should decide which operations are useful; deterministic runtime
metadata should decide whether their executions may overlap.

### Errors are observations unless they break the runtime

A malformed argument, command failure, or unavailable tool is often useful
feedback for replanning. Codex can turn an ordinary tool failure into a tool
result the model can inspect. A fatal invariant violation instead terminates the
sampling path. This distinction prevents both extremes: crashing on every tool
error and hiding genuine harness corruption inside natural-language feedback.

### Hooks are middleware, not policy by prompt

Pre-tool hooks can block or transform a request; post-tool hooks can attach
feedback or additional context. They provide deterministic extension points
around the side-effect boundary. Importantly, a post-tool hook cannot undo an
already executed side effect, so precondition checks belong before execution.

## 7. Security Is the Intersection of Controls

No single “safe mode” is enough. Codex composes several mechanisms:

| Mechanism | Question answered |
|---|---|
| OS sandbox | What files, processes, and network resources are technically reachable? |
| Approval policy | When must authority return to a human or reviewer? |
| Execution rules | Which known command patterns may run, prompt, or be blocked? |
| Managed network policy | Which destinations are allowed or require review? |
| Tool-specific policy | What constraints apply to MCP or other external capabilities? |
| Telemetry | What happened, under whose request, and with what decision? |

The effective action set is the intersection

$$
\mathcal A_{\text{effective}}
=
\mathcal A_{\text{sandbox}}
\cap
\mathcal A_{\text{approval}}
\cap
\mathcal A_{\text{rules}}
\cap
\mathcal A_{\text{tool}}.
$$

This separation matters because prompting only influences model behavior; it
does not create a hard resource boundary. Conversely, a sandbox alone cannot
decide whether sending a message or changing a production record is authorized.

One subtle but general lesson from the
[agent-loop description](https://openai.com/index/unrolling-the-codex-agent-loop/)
is that Codex's local shell sandbox does not automatically wrap arbitrary MCP
tools. Each external tool provider must enforce its own constraints. A harness
should never advertise “the agent is sandboxed” without naming which capability
is actually inside which boundary.

OpenAI's deployment guidance adds two production practices: avoid open-ended
outbound network access, and combine endpoint security alerts with agent-native
logs that preserve the surrounding user intent, tool activity, approvals, and
network decisions. See
[Running Codex safely at OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/running-codex-safely/).

## 8. Event-Driven State Makes Clients Replaceable

Codex app-server uses requests for commands and notifications for lifecycle
changes. The client does not need to infer hidden state from terminal text; it
can observe explicit thread, turn, item, approval, and completion events.

This yields a useful split:

```text
command:      "start this turn" or "approve this action"
event:        "turn started", "item completed", or "turn interrupted"
projection:   what a TUI, IDE, app, or orchestrator displays
```

Durable rollout records are written as JSONL and can be replayed or inspected.
The state layer also indexes thread metadata for listing and resumption. This is
event-sourcing-like without requiring every derived UI state to be written into
the model conversation.

Why this matters:

- clients can disconnect and rehydrate state
- CLI, IDE, and app surfaces can share a core runtime
- tests can assert lifecycle events rather than scrape prose
- interruption and partial completion become explicit states
- protocol evolution becomes a compatibility problem that can be tested

The source repository's own review guidance treats app-server APIs, raw response
events, configuration, CLI parameters, and rollout resumption as external
compatibility surfaces. That is a strong harness-engineering principle: **the
protocol is part of the product, not incidental glue**.

## 9. Persistence, Resumption, and Steering

Long-running work should expect process death, client disconnection, user
course-correction, and context replacement. Codex supports these cases with:

- append-only rollout records
- thread resume and fork operations
- history reconstruction
- explicit interruption markers
- in-flight steering for regular turns
- background process handles and cancellation tokens
- separate stored artifacts in the workspace

A robust turn is therefore not a blocking function call. It is a resumable state
machine:

$$
z_{t+1}
=
F(z_t,\text{command},\text{event}),
$$

where $z_t$ includes the active turn, history position, running tools,
permission state, and client-visible lifecycle.

The practical lesson is to design interruption semantics early. “Cancel” must
define what happens to the model stream, in-flight tool, already completed side
effects, stored history, and next resumption. Killing a process is not a full
cancellation design.

## 10. Skills, Plugins, MCP, and Subagents

These mechanisms operate at different abstraction levels:

| Mechanism | Adds | Main risk |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction file | repository-local constraints and conventions | stale or conflicting context |
| Skill | reusable procedure plus selected resources | loading too much context |
| Plugin | packaged skills, hooks, tools, or integrations | dependency and permission expansion |
| MCP server | external tool/resource interface | trust boundary and side effects |
| Subagent | another model trajectory with separate context | coordination and duplicated work |

The architectural insight is **progressive capability disclosure**. A small
stable description can tell the model what exists; detailed instructions and
heavy resources are loaded only when selected. This saves tokens and reduces
irrelevant instruction interference.

Subagents are implemented as managed child threads rather than magical extra
reasoning. Their benefit comes from parallel compute and context isolation; their
cost comes from communication, synchronization, and merge conflicts. They are
most useful when work can be partitioned with explicit inputs and inspectable
outputs.

## 11. What Codex Adds to the Generic Harness Picture

The generic [Agent Harness](harness.qmd) note explains the components. Codex
adds several concrete engineering lessons:

| Generic principle | Codex realization | Broader lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Compile context | layered instructions plus per-step world-state diffs | context has authority, provenance, and cache cost |
| Route tools | typed, namespaced router and registry | separate model-visible schemas from runtimes |
| Control side effects | sandbox, approvals, rules, hooks, network policy | safety is an intersection of controls |
| Preserve state | JSONL rollouts plus indexed thread state | make histories replayable and derived views rebuildable |
| Support feedback | streaming events, tool results, steering, cancellation | turns are interactive state machines |
| Parallelize safely | per-tool concurrency declaration | concurrency belongs in capability metadata |
| Serve many clients | versioned app-server protocol | keep the core loop independent from presentation |
| Manage cost | stable prompt prefixes and automatic compaction | optimize cached inference, not token count alone |

The most important synthesis is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{reliable autonomy}
=
\text{semantic flexibility inside deterministic boundaries}
}.
$$

## 12. What the Source Does Not Prove

Reading the harness cannot answer every question about Codex performance:

- It does not reveal the proprietary model's training data or complete
  post-training recipe.
- Code presence does not show which feature is enabled in every product or
  account.
- A configurable mechanism does not establish its production configuration.
- End-to-end benchmark gains cannot be assigned to the model or harness without
  controlled ablations.
- A large mature codebase contains compatibility layers and experiments; not
  every module is a timeless design recommendation.

Separate three kinds of claims when reading an agent repository:

1. **mechanism:** the source can do this
2. **configuration:** a deployment enables it this way
3. **effect:** enabling it causally improves quality, cost, or safety

Source inspection is strongest for the first and needs documentation,
telemetry, or experiments for the other two.

## 13. Interview Questions

- What exactly is open-source when someone says “Codex is open-source”?
- Why separate a thread, a user turn, and a model sampling step?
- Why should a tool call retain the step context that advertised it?
- How does deterministic tool ordering affect inference cost?
- Why are ordinary tool failures returned to the model while fatal runtime
  failures terminate the turn?
- What can an OS sandbox enforce that an approval policy cannot, and vice versa?
- Why does sandboxing a shell tool not automatically sandbox an MCP tool?
- When may two tool calls run concurrently?
- Why is an event protocol better than scraping terminal output?
- What state is needed to resume correctly after interruption?
- Which parts of Codex are model intelligence, and which are harness
  intelligence?
- How would you ablate model and harness changes to attribute a quality gain?

## 14. Exercises

- [ ] Trace one function call from streamed response item through routing,
  execution, and returned observation.
- [ ] Draw the state transitions for start, steer, interrupt, and resume.
- [ ] Design a tool concurrency declaration for read, edit, test, and deploy.
- [ ] Specify a permission profile using sandbox, approval, and network rules.
- [ ] Implement an append-only rollout and reconstruct a thread from it.
- [ ] Measure prompt-cache hits before and after randomizing tool order.
- [ ] Compare failure recovery with and without durable artifacts.
